newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi to start bilateral WTO talks next year.
newsitem.headline: Saudi to start bilateral WTO talks next year.

text.p: Saudi Arabia will start bilateral talks on commerical issues with some members of the World Trade Organisation early in 1998, part of a bid to join the world body, the Industry and Electricity Minister said on Tuesday.
Hashem bin Abdullah bin Hashem Yamani said in an interview with the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) that he expected the bilateral talks to "last for some time".

"He (Yamani) expected the kingdom to start at the beginning of 1998 bilateral negotiations with some WTO member states that had asked to discuss with the kingdom some commercial issues including custom tariffs and foreign investment in the services sector," SPA said.
Yamani said his ministry was preparing a study on a new industrial policy in the oil-rich kingdom "to meet the new international climate and future challenges".
He said the kingdom needed "to develop industrial policy and improve the investment climate to encourage both national and foreign investment in national industry".
Saudi Arabia says it hopes to join the WTO as an observer next year and become a full member by the year 2002.
The world's largest oil producer applied in 1993 to join the trade watchdog's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). They have since held three rounds of talks.
Trade diplomats reported progress in the discussions after the third round of talks in May but said Saudi Arabia must do more to present detailed offers on market access.
Concerns by trading partners include Riyadh's restrictions on import licensing in areas such as chemicals, pasteurised milk, information technology products and farm equipment.

Saudi Arabia is eager to diversify its oil-dependent economy and is seeking to join the WTO on the favourable terms granted to developing countries. It has repeatedly said it was taking measures to encourage foreign inflows, including steps to provide protection for foreign investment and ease bureaucratic obstacles in the licensing of foreign projects.
It is also reviewing its foreign capital law to introduce more incentives to foreign investors in a country where most foreign capital is invested in joint ventures with Saudi firms.
